strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: self-verification for small language models under test-time compute scaling, where larger verifiers undermine efficiency benefits.
Proposes a simple and intuitive two-stage verification method: a tool-based filter followed by an RM-based scorer, compatible with both PRMs and generative verifiers via distillation and multi-LoRA.
Provides theoretical motivation showing that tool access can reduce memorization demands and that improving verifier noise can improve best-of-N performance.
Empirical evaluation covers multiple benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), several small models, and comparisons against majority voting, zero-shot GenRM, and distilled PRM/GenRM baselines.
Includes useful analyses such as category/difficulty breakdowns, verifier-size scaling, filter behavior, data efficiency, and success/failure case studies.
Limitations and failure modes are explicitly acknowledged, including false negatives from ToolV and the narrow best-of-N setting.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: tool integration for reasoning and reward modeling is already explored in prior work (e.g., PAL, ToRA, tool-augmented reward modeling); applying tools specifically to small-model self-verification is a natural but not deeply novel extension.

The headline claim that a 1B model with T1 outperforms Llama-3.1 8B relies on comparing best-of-64 decoding against greedy 8B decoding; the 8B model is not given comparable test-time compute, so the claim is overstated.

Missing important baselines: tool-integrated generation (e.g., PAL/ToRA-style solving with code execution) followed by majority voting or verifier selection, and larger verifiers evaluated under the same best-of-N protocol.

The theoretical analysis is loose and toy: it assumes perfect tool access/execution and ignores the difficulty of learning to generate correct tool calls; Theorem 5.3 assumes q fixed while ToolV can reduce recall and thus harm q, so the monotonicity result does not fully capture the practical trade-off.

Evaluation lacks statistical significance/error bars and cost/latency analysis for tool calls, which matter for small-model deployment; MMLU-Pro results are mixed and depend on retrieved document quality, with strong gains only using gold documents.

Several implementation details are unclear or incompletely specified, including handling of cases where all candidates are filtered out and precise aggregation in weighted Best-of-N; reproducibility is limited by lack of code release and reliance on proprietary teacher models.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: self-verification for test-time scaling in small language models, where reliance on large verifiers undermines efficiency.
Proposes an intuitive two-stage framework that combines tool execution/filtering with reward-model scoring and distillation.

Evaluates on multiple benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro) and several small models (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen-2.5-0.5B, SmolLM2-360M), with analyses by problem category, difficulty, verifier size, and tool filtering.
Provides theoretical attempts to explain reduced memorization via tools and improved best-of-N performance under a better verifier.
Includes useful practical observations, e.g., a code interpreter substantially helps arithmetic verification, and ToolV can improve PRM/GenRM under limited distillation data.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: tool-augmented reasoning, program-aided language models, code-execution verification, and tool-augmented reward modeling are already well established; using code execution to check arithmetic verification is largely expected rather than surprising.

The paper claims self-verification and reduced dependence on larger models, but the method heavily depends on large teacher models for distillation (GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B) and external tools. Thus it is not truly small-model self-verification, and the comparison to larger-model dependence is not clean.

Experimental comparisons are not fully fair: larger models are compared only at N=1/greedy decoding, not under similar test-time compute or Best-of-N settings; no same-compute or same-tool baselines are reported.

Missing controls and ablations: tool-only verification, code execution without distilled RM, RM without tools, and the separate effects of teacher distillation versus tool use are not adequately isolated. Gains may be confounded by code filtering and additional teacher supervision.

Evaluation protocol is questionable: for math, ToolV generates 4 code completions and passes if at least one says the solution is correct, which can increase false positives; for knowledge tasks, it uses retrieved/gold documents. Exact tables, variance, and statistical significance are mostly absent.

The theoretical analysis is extremely toy and does not model realistic code generation errors, execution failures, retrieval noise, or learned tool-use. The claim that tool access reduces memorization to zero ignores the need for the small model to generate correct tool calls.
MMLU-Pro results are narrow and unstable, limited to a few domains with weak retrieved-document quality; the gold-document upper-bound experiment does not demonstrate a deployable solution.

The method is essentially a rejection filter and cannot recover false negatives. This is acknowledged but not addressed, and reported improvements may be fragile when code generation or retrieval fails.
Clarity and writing issues, including typos ('fack-checking', 'memorization-heay', 'eqation', 'is.correct'), inconsistent notation, and insufficient methodological precision, reduce confidence.
Reproducibility is limited: no code/data release, reliance on hosted teacher models, and insufficient artifact details make exact replication difficult.

Positioning relative to existing tool-integrated reward models and program-aided verification is insufficient; the paper does not convincingly establish what is fundamentally new beyond combining known components.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely problem: whether small language models can self-verify under test-time compute scaling, and proposes tool integration as a practical remedy.
Presents a clean two-stage method (tool-based verifier filter plus reward-model scoring) that can integrate with both PRM and GenRM verifiers and uses multi-LoRA distillation.
Includes a theoretical analysis linking tool use to reduced memorization demands and monotonicity of best-of-N performance under an imperfect verifier, which helps motivate the method.
Evaluates on multiple benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro) and several small models, with comparisons to majority voting, zero-shot GenRM, and distilled PRM/GenRM baselines.
Provides implementation details, training hyperparameters, prompts, and additional analyses such as category-level performance, data efficiency, and failure cases.
The empirical gains, especially on MATH500, are meaningful and support the claim that tool-integrated verification can substantially improve small-model test-time scaling.
weaknesses: The headline comparison that a 1B model with T1 outperforms an 8B model is potentially misleading: the 8B result appears to be greedy N=1 while the 1B result uses Best-of-N scaling, so the comparison is not at matched test-time compute or matched scaling budget.
The evaluation lacks a clean ablation of ToolV alone versus ToolV plus RM-based verifier; it is difficult to fully separate the contribution of the tool filter from the reward model and distillation.

The theoretical analysis relies on idealized assumptions: Theorem 5.2 assumes the tool function is exactly correct, while the actual ToolV relies on generated code or fact-checking that can be wrong; Theorem 5.3 models changes in true-negative probability but does not account for increased false negatives caused by the filter.

ToolV can reject correct solutions due to faulty generated code or retrieval/verification errors, and the main results do not systematically quantify how much this false-negative behavior harms best-of-N performance across models and datasets.

The MMLU-Pro evaluation is limited to one small model and uses retrieved documents plus GPT-4o-generated gold documents as an upper bound, which may overstate realistic performance and does not fully establish broad multi-domain generalization.

Some implementation and presentation details are weak: the paper includes invalid Python snippets in examples (e.g., is.correct, eqation) and several typos, and there is no clear code release, which may hinder reproducibility.
The weighted Best-of-N evaluation protocol is nonstandard and would benefit from clearer justification and comparison to standard Best-of-N or majority-vote aggregation.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: whether small language models can reliably verify outputs for test-time compute scaling, and how tool integration can close the gap to larger verifiers.

Proposes a clear and simple two-stage framework, Tool-integrated Verification (T1), that filters candidates with external tools and then uses a distilled reward model or generative verifier for scoring; the framework is compatible with both PRMs and GenRMs.

Provides extensive empirical evidence across multiple small models (SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B), datasets (MATH500, GSM8K, and a subset of MMLU-Pro), and verifier types, showing consistent improvements over majority voting, distilled verifiers, zero-shot GenRM, and Themis.
Demonstrates practically meaningful gains, e.g., a 1B model with ToolV can surpass an 8B model under greedy decoding on MATH500, and 1B GenRM + ToolV can outperform an 8B GenRM verifier.
Includes useful analyses of problem category/difficulty, data efficiency, compute overhead, and ablation of the two-stage design, which help support the main claims.
Reproducibility is reasonably addressed with detailed hyperparameters, prompts, training settings, and a promise to release scripts and seeds.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: tool-augmented verification and tool-integrated reward modeling have been explored before (e.g., Themis); the main new element is applying similar ideas to small language models under test-time scaling, which is useful but incremental.

The theoretical analysis is weak and disconnected from the actual method. Lemma 5.1 largely imports an existing learning-theoretic bound; Theorem 5.2 is almost trivial given an exact tool; Theorem 5.3 is a known monotonicity result for noisy verifiers. It does not rigorously justify the two-stage ToolV+RM framework for real LLMs, despite the abstract's claim of proof/guarantee.

The empirical evaluation is mostly limited to mathematical reasoning, with MMLU-Pro only as a small appendixed subset. Generalization to broader reasoning, fact-checking, and tool-use domains is not strongly established.

Baselines and comparisons are reasonable but not fully exhaustive: the paper does not compare against a larger verifier (e.g., 8B GenRM/PRM) also equipped with ToolV, making it less clear whether the gains come from tool integration specifically or from comparing a tool-augmented small model to a non-tool larger model.

The tool-based verifier relies on generated Python code, and the paper reports relatively low recall, meaning correct solutions can be mistakenly filtered out. This false-negative issue is acknowledged as a limitation but not solved or deeply analyzed.

Main results appear to lack error bars or multi-seed variance reporting, making it harder to assess the statistical robustness of some reported gains, especially on the noisier knowledge-intensive tasks.
Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, particularly the implication that the theoretical results guarantee improved test-time scaling for real small language models.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question: whether small language models can serve as reliable verifiers for test-time compute scaling.
Identifies memorization-heavy verification steps, such as arithmetic and fact-checking, as a plausible bottleneck for sLMs.
Proposes a simple and intuitive two-stage framework that combines external tools with PRM/GenRM verification.
Includes experiments on multiple small model families and two math benchmarks, with additional appendices on prompts, hyperparameters, and qualitative cases.
Provides some supporting analyses, such as category/difficulty breakdowns, data efficiency, and compute-budget discussion.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: tool-augmented verification and program-aided checking are well-established; the two-stage tool-filter-then-reward-model design is incremental over existing tool-integrated reward modeling and program-aided reasoning work.

The theoretical analysis is weak and largely disconnected from the method. Lemma 5.1 imports an existing memorization bound for a toy addition task, and its cardinality calculation is imprecise. Theorem 5.2 is essentially tautological: if theta is independent of data, mutual information is zero. Theorem 5.3 studies a simplified binary verifier and does not model false negatives, tool errors, or the actual two-stage filtering behavior.

The central empirical claim that a 1B model with T1 outperforms an 8B model is based on comparing a test-time-scaled 1B model against an 8B model evaluated only with greedy decoding or N=1, which is not an apples-to-apples comparison. The 8B model is not given the same test-time compute budget.
Evaluation is narrow: the main experiments focus on MATH500 and GSM8K, with only a small MMLU-Pro subset in the appendix. Broader reasoning or knowledge-intensive benchmarks are missing.

Baselines and ablations are incomplete. The paper does not compare against strong existing tool-integrated verifiers beyond Themis, nor does it thoroughly ablate the two stages under matched compute. The claimed advantage over simply scaling verifier size is not fully isolated.

The reported gains from adding ToolV to PRM/GenRM are sometimes small, especially on GSM8K, and the two-stage design only marginally improves over ToolV alone in some ablations. This weakens the claim that both stages are necessary.

ToolV relies on generated Python code and code execution for math verification. The paper acknowledges false negatives from incorrect generated code, but the main results may be sensitive to prompt design, code-generation quality, and execution rules. This sensitivity is not sufficiently stress-tested.
Reproducibility is only partially supported: prompts and hyperparameters are provided, but no code package is available, and some dataset construction and evaluation details remain unclear.

Writing and presentation contain several errors and inconsistencies, such as concept-proof instead of proof-of-concept, fack-checking, inconsistent naming T1/T1, and imprecise descriptions of baselines and metrics.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important question: whether small language models can reliably verify candidate outputs for test-time compute scaling, without relying on a much larger verifier.

Proposes T1, a simple and intuitive two-stage framework that first uses external tools (e.g., code interpreter, retriever) to filter memorization-heavy verification errors and then applies a small reward model or generative verifier; the framework integrates with both PRM and GenRM.
Includes motivating concept-proof experiments showing that small LMs degrade on arithmetic verification as the number of operands grows, while code execution largely mitigates this gap.

Reports consistent empirical gains on MATH500 and GSM8K across three small models (SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B), with both PRM and GenRM, and provides additional ablations on data efficiency, MMLU-Pro, and compute scaling.

Provides a theory-inspired framing, including memorization-bound arguments and a monotonicity result for best-of-N under imperfect verification, plus detailed implementation/reproducibility information and prompts.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: tool-augmented reward modeling/verification has been explored before (e.g., Themis), and the proposed two-stage filter-then-score pipeline is straightforward; the theoretical results are highly idealized and partly tautological under their assumptions.

Evaluation is narrow: the main experiments focus on MATH500 and GSM8K, with MMLU-Pro only in the appendix; only parallel best-of-N scaling is studied, leaving sequential/beam/search-based test-time scaling unexplored.

Baselines and comparisons are incomplete: the paper does not compare against tool-integrated generation methods such as ToRA/PAL, nor against a larger model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B) under the same test-time compute budget or with tools; the headline claim that a 1B model outperforms an 8B model is mainly against 8B greedy decoding, not 8B with comparable scaling.

The theoretical analysis does not adequately model practical failure modes of ToolV: Theorem 5.2 assumes a perfect tool call and I(X;theta|P)=0, ignoring remaining memorization needed for code generation/tool invocation; Theorem 5.3 assumes fixed verifier acceptance behavior and does not account for the false negatives observed in Table 4 (low recall), which can filter out correct solutions.

ToolV can reject correct solutions due to erroneous generated code; although acknowledged in the limitations and case analysis, this limitation is not thoroughly quantified for the final best-of-N accuracy or for cases where all correct candidates are filtered out.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially 'tool integration is necessary' and the broad superiority over larger models; the paper would benefit from fairer compute-normalized and same-model-family comparisons.

Presentation and reproducibility details are somewhat uneven: there are typos, unclear/duplicated figures in the extracted version, and reliance on gpt-4o-mini-generated supervision, which may limit reproducibility and generalizability.
